system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2185-07-19 02:55:00 to 2185-07-19 18:29:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex history of gastroparesis, sclerosing mesenteritis, and G-tube dependence was readmitted within 24 hours of discharge due to recurrent severe nausea and vomiting of 6 liters of dark green emesis. She reported feeling isolated and anxious about her care. During the 14-day admission, her G-tube was replaced with a Wills-Ogelsby tube, which improved gastric venting and reduced symptoms. TPN was restarted via a femoral line after insurance approval. Nausea was managed with Phenergan and Ativan, while dronabinol was discontinued due to sedation. Abdominal imaging showed no obstruction, and labs remained stable. The patient expressed emotional distress, and mental health support was provided for dysthymia and suicidal ideation. She was discharged home with a plan for nightly TPN, visiting nurse visits, and close follow-up.
problems: Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Migraine with aura, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus
Disorder of bone and cartilage, unspecified
Surgical operation with formation of external stoma causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of operation

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with some fevers and a red area near your line. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this morning I noticed a pink spot near my femoral line. It was tender and had some crusting. After dinner, I felt dizzy and my sons saw me shivering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You said your temperature peaked at 99.7°F. Did you take anything for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t take anything. I just kept checking it every 20 minutes. I didn’t want to come to the hospital, but my sons insisted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing the right thing by getting it checked. We’re concerned about a possible infection at your line site. We’ve started antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about losing the line. It’s my only access for TPN. My arms are all scarred over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know how important it is. The line doesn’t look infected along the tunnel, and you’re not running a high fever. We’re going to try to keep it in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve been doing dressing changes, but my husband used to do them. I’ve only done it twice myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You explained the steps well. We’ll have a nurse come in the morning to help train your caregiver. We want to make sure it’s done safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures are still pending, but you’re afebrile and the line site looks stable. We’re going to treat the redness with topical bacitracin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe to use with my allergies? I’m allergic to a lot of things—sulfa, Bactrim, even Lovenox.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bacitracin is safe. It’s not related to the antibiotics you’re allergic to. We’ll apply it only to the small area of redness during dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also felt confused last night, and my vision was blurry. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it might be from the alprazolam you took. It can cause drowsiness and confusion, especially with your other medications. We recommend stopping it for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take it for anxiety. My husband passed away recently, and I’ve been struggling. I don’t want to feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll keep your other anxiety meds like lorazepam and paroxetine. Please follow up with your psychiatrist to adjust your treatment safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your condition has improved. The redness is still there but not worse. We’ll send you home with instructions to continue the bacitracin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re still pending. If they come back positive, your doctor will contact you. For now, we’ll monitor at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I can go home. I just want to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your enoxaparin dose adjusted to 30 mg twice daily for better clot prevention. And remember—no alprazolam until you speak with your provider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my sons will help with the dressing changes now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. A visiting nurse will also check in to help with the line care and monitor the redness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really scared I’d lose the line or get really sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re being very proactive. We’ll make sure you have all the support you need at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. It means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be discharged soon. Keep taking your other medications as prescribed, and call if the redness spreads or you develop a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex medical history including sclerosing mesenteritis and long-term TPN dependence via a femoral line was admitted for evaluation of fever and redness at her line site. She reported mild erythema and tenderness, with no high fever or systemic symptoms. Blood cultures were drawn and antibiotics initiated, but the line was preserved due to her limited venous access. The redness was treated with topical bacitracin. She experienced transient confusion and diplopia, likely due to alprazolam, which was discontinued. She remained stable, mental status cleared, and was discharged home with a visiting nurse to assist with dressing changes and monitor for infection. Blood and urine cultures remained pending at discharge.
